question_text: A retail company stores 50TB of historical transaction data in Amazon S3 as gzipped CSV files; data scientists report that SageMaker training jobs spend most of their time loading and parsing data rather than training. The team will run dozens of experiments per week against the same dataset filtered by transaction date. Which approach will most improve training read performance while reducing storage cost?
explanation: Parquet is a columnar format that supports compression and predicate pushdown; partitioning by date lets training jobs read only the relevant partitions which dramatically reduces I/O and storage costs. CSV with more instances does not reduce parsing overhead or scan cost. JSON Lines is row-based and verbose so it does not help with read performance and EFS is much more expensive than S3 for read-mostly ML datasets. FSx for Lustre is useful but does not solve the inefficient CSV format and increases cost compared to optimizing the format in S3.
option_text: Keep the CSV format and increase the number of training instances to parallelize reads

question_text: A finance team uses Amazon Athena to query a 4PB S3 data lake of trade data for ML feature generation; queries scan terabytes per run and costs have grown sharply. Balancing the entire dataset before splitting causes leakage. Drop Duplicate Rows on the label column is irrelevant. One-Hot Encode on the label column is irrelevant for binary class imbalance.
option_text: Apply Drop Duplicate Rows on the label column to balance classes

question_text: A team uses SageMaker Feature Store to feed a hiring-recommendation model; auditors require ongoing monitoring for representation imbalance on protected attributes across the feature group used for retraining. Which approach best meets this requirement?
explanation: Scheduling Clarify pre-training bias jobs against the offline store of the feature group provides recurring measurement of representation imbalance on protected attributes - the offline store is the analytics-friendly persisted record of feature history. question_text: A computer-vision team is designing an end-to-end pipeline that must ingest new product images from store cameras into a governed data lake; label them with quality controls; engineer image-derived features for both training and online inference; and provide pre-training fairness checks before retraining. Which architecture best satisfies all four requirements?
explanation: S3 with Lake Formation governance addresses the ingestion-and-governance requirement (TS1.1); Ground Truth with multi-worker labels and consolidation addresses labeling quality (TS1.3); Feature Store online and offline stores share a single feature definition for inference and training (TS1.2); Clarify pre-training bias jobs cover the fairness audit before retraining (TS1.3). The other options each violate one or more of these requirements - DynamoDB with manual spreadsheet labels misses governance and quality; public S3 with no labeling tool misses both; FSx-as-lake with Athena for online lookup violates the online-inference latency need.
option_text: DynamoDB-only image storage; spreadsheet labeling; nightly CSV exports for inference; Macie for fairness checks

question_text: An ML platform team is publishing standards for production ML data pipelines covering ingestion preparation and integrity. The standards must align with AWS best practices and apply consistently across teams. Which TWO standards are correct? (Select TWO)
explanation: The Glue Schema Registry enforces schema compatibility at the ingestion layer (TS1.1) while Glue Data Quality enforces validity and integrity at the preparation layer (TS1.3) - together they form a durable contract across pipeline stages; Feature Store with paired online and offline stores ensures that features used for training (TS1.2) match those used for inference avoiding training-serving skew (TS1.2). Letting each team invent its own conventions is the anti-pattern these standards are meant to replace. Encrypting only at rest leaves in-transit data exposed. Random-shuffle splits for time series leak future information into training and produce optimistic offline metrics.
option_text: Use Glue Schema Registry compatibility rules at the ingestion layer and Glue Data Quality rule evaluations at the preparation layer to fail pipelines on critical regressions
